tracks.body:
# AI PM Weekly Briefing — Vocal Media

*Framed for AI content pipelines, creator/editorial tooling, and audience automation. Bias toward building AI product judgment.*

---

### 1. Evals are the new PRDs (Amplitude's build-in-public account)
Amplitude's team describes a three-phase approach where 

evaluations become the new PRDs, first using evals to define the core use cases and requirements that guide how AI agents are built, tuned, and improved, then empowering the broadest set of SMEs and product teams to create and maintain them.

 They also warn that 

teams building AI products need more humans in the loop, not fewer, to handle the complexity of evals, integrations, and the constant iteration required to ship real value.

**Why it matters:** For Vocal's content pipelines, this reframes your job — instead of writing a spec and handing off, you write the definition of "good output" and grow it as new failure modes appear. It also argues against thin, fully-autonomous editorial automation with no review layer.

**Source:** Amplitude — https://amplitude.com/blog/ai-product-learnings-2025

---

### 2. A real shipped-product story: Productboard Spark
This is a candid post-mortem-plus-playbook. The author admits 

they did not have quality out of the gate with their first generative AI product, launched before quality was consistent enough to build user trust, and that expectations outpaced what the technology could deliver.

 The fix, applied to their next product: 

rigorous evals, stricter quality gates, and systematic improvement before each release stage.

 To decide readiness, they 

used a combination of engaged user metrics and AI quality evaluation scores to measure quality and determine when they were ready to move between thresholds.

**Why it matters:** A concrete model for how to stage a creator-facing AI feature — pair user engagement signals with quality scores as gates, rather than shipping on a good demo. Directly relevant to launching editorial or audience-automation tools where a bad first impression erodes creator trust.

**Source:** Ravi Mehta's blog — https://blog.ravi-mehta.com/p/building-ai-products-lessons-from

---

### 3. How to measure AI success: the four-layer pyramid
This guide organizes AI measurement into layers. 

Effective AI product measurement requires four distinct layers, each serving a different purpose — think of them as a pyramid: start at the top with user outcomes and only dig deeper to diagnose issues. These are your north star metrics, answering "did we solve the user's problem?"

 The key discipline: 

define success precisely — "user clicked the button" is not success, it's activity; success is the outcome they came for.

 It centers on Task Success Rate and User Acceptance Rate (how often users act on AI suggestions).

**Why it matters:** For Vocal, "content generated" is activity; "content published and kept by the creator" is the real outcome. User Acceptance Rate is a clean north-star candidate for any AI drafting or editing feature.

**Source:** Institute of Product Management — https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/ai-product-metrics

---

### 4. Framework: link evals to business impact (don't measure in a vacuum)
A practical method for connecting model quality to real results. Start with critical user journeys, then 

map each desired outcome to leading and lagging metrics: leading metrics are your evaluation metrics (response accuracy on a curated test set, latency, hallucination rate), and lagging metrics are the business KPIs these drive (user satisfaction ratings, conversion rate, support ticket volume).

 Also useful: 

connect outcomes to behavior — if the AI's suggestion was accepted, log success; if users ignored or reversed it, log failure. That links evals to business impact.

**Why it matters:** Gives you a defensible way to argue for AI investment to leadership — you can tie a hallucination-rate improvement to a downstream editorial or audience metric instead of reporting model stats no one can interpret.

**Source:** Product School — https://productschool.com/blog/artificial-intelligence/evaluation-metrics

---

### 5. How the AI PM role is actually being scoped
Useful for understanding your own mandate and career path. One recruiter observes that 

an AI product manager in 2026 is one of four working roles: the copilot PM who owns a customer-facing LLM surface, the AI platform PM who owns the internal model and tooling layer, the ML feature PM who ships model-powered features inside a non-AI product, or the AI ops PM who deploys AI to a non-engineering team.

 The bar for hiring: 

grading model-evaluation fluency, data instincts, and the willingness to kill a feature that demos beautifully and fails in production — pattern recognition on shipped product work matters more than the logo on the resume.

**Why it matters:** Your Vocal role blends the "ML feature PM" and "AI ops PM" archetypes (creator tooling plus internal editorial/audience automation). Knowing which surfaces you own — and building an eval-set story around them — is how the role is judged industry-wide.

**Source:** KORE1 — https://www.kore1.com/how-to-hire-ai-product-manager-2026/

---

### 6. Tactic to apply this week: the 30-minute eval
A lightweight, repeatable habit. The recipe: 

choose one AI feature your team has shipped in the past month, schedule 30 minutes this week to run an evaluation, and don't wait for perfect conditions or more comprehensive data — use what you have.

 It names three traps to avoid: 

the Dashboard Trap (tracking engagement while ignoring whether the AI actually works), the Technical Handoff (assuming model metrics like F1 translate to user value — they often don't), and the Ship-and-Hope Method (relying on user complaints to surface issues).

 A complementary version: 

pick one AI feature, define what "good" means for five to ten real inputs, and run an eval — you'll learn more from one run than from weeks of manual testing.

**Why it matters:** This is the single most actionable item here. Pick one live Vocal feature (a headline generator, a tagging model, a recommendation surface), define "good" on ~10 real creator examples, and run it before Friday. It converts 

"I think it's better" into "we tested 200 cases and accuracy improved 5% without regressing tone."

**Sources:** Sid Saladi (Substack) — https://sidsaladi.substack.com/p/pms-30-minute-ai-evals-a-lightweight · Braintrust — https://www.braintrust.dev/blog/evals-for-pms

tracks.body:
# This Week in Claude & AI Automation

## 1. Live artifacts now call MCP connectors on every view — build a self-updating dashboard from one prompt

Anthropic shipped the missing piece in Claude Code's July 13–17 update. 

A published Claude Code Artifact can now call MCP connectors every time someone views it, so the page shows live data — and can even take actions — instead of a frozen snapshot from the session that built it.

 

Artifacts use the viewers' own MCP connectors, so creators don't need to re-run sessions to refresh, and viewers can only see the data they have access to.

**Try this** — In a Cowork/Claude Code session with your GitHub (or HubSpot/Linear/Stripe) connector active, paste:

> `Build a dashboard artifact of our open pull requests that pulls the live list through my GitHub connector when the page loads. For each connector block, include fallback copy if the connector isn't connected. Prefer SVG and CSS over inlined PNGs to stay under the render cap.`

Two gotchas worth knowing before you ship: 

a connector-backed dashboard cannot be a public link on any plan

, and 

read-only SQL queries can still trigger per-call Allow/Deny gates when a tool like execute_sql is classified as write-capable — treat connector tool permissions as per-artifact-context, not guaranteed to inherit global "Always Allow" settings.

**Source:** Claude Code Docs / Digital Applied — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/artifacts · https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/live-client-dashboards-claude-artifacts-mcp

---

## 2. Subagent nesting caps changed three times in four days — audit your background spend

If you run fan-out workflows, the guardrails just moved under you. 

On July 21, version 2.1.217 capped concurrently-running subagents at 20 and stopped subagents from spawning nested subagents at all. On July 24, version 2.1.219 reinstated nesting at a default depth of 3.

 Critically, 

a budget-cap bug that let background agents spend past the limit got fixed

 in the same window — meaning anything you ran under `--max-budget-usd` before July 21 may have overspent.

**Try this** — Two concrete actions:
1. Audit spend from any background-agent runs made under `--max-budget-usd` **before July 21, 2026**, since the cap wasn't enforced then.
2. To lock nesting back down for predictable cost, set in your `settings.json`:

```json
{ "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH": "1" } }
```

Subagents can now spawn nested subagents up to depth 3 by default; set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1 to disable nesting.

**Source:** Digital Applied / Claude Code Changelog — https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/claude-code-subagent-depth-limits-budget-caps-2026

---

## 3. Undocumented "observer agents" — a watchdog subagent that flags drift while a worker runs

This one isn't in the docs or changelog. 

Claude Code observer agents are a new subagent role that watches another agent while it works and speaks up only when something is going wrong. Anthropic shipped the feature into the binary sometime in early July 2026, gated it behind an experimental flag, and said nothing.

 The pattern: a worker does the task, and 

the observer reads a read-only feed of everything the worker does

 to catch it going off-track.

**Try this** — Get the flag name exactly right (early write-ups botch it). In `settings.json`:

```json
{ "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_OBSERVER_AGENTS": "1" } }
```

Early write-ups have been dropping the CODE_ segment and calling it CLAUDE_EXPERIMENTAL_OBSERVER_AGENTS, which does nothing. The real variable is CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_OBSERVER_AGENTS.

 Then 

attach an observer through the front matter of the agent you want watched — the watched agent declares a single field naming its observer's type.

 One caveat: 

a server-side gate (tengu_observer_agents_enabled) is on by default, but Anthropic can flip it for a cohort or kill it entirely from the server, so treat availability as provisional.

**Source:** ClaudeFast — https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/agents/observer-agents

---

## 4. The generate → grade → regenerate loop — a rubric second-pass that lifts output quality with no model change

This is a shipping automation pattern, not a think-piece. 

Once your task agent finishes, that output gets handed to a separate grading agent. The grading agent reads the output, reads your rubric, and scores how well the output matches. If the score is below threshold, it can flag the specific issues and kick the task back for another run.

 Anthropic's Outcomes feature reported 

+8.4% task success on .docx outputs and +10.1% on .pptx outputs

 from this loop alone. But you don't need the managed platform — 

you don't need managed agents to implement the generate-grade-regenerate loop.

**Try this** — Wire this as a second Claude call after your generation step:

> `You are a grading agent. Score the OUTPUT below against each rubric criterion independently. For each, return PASS/FAIL and one sentence of evidence.`
> `Rubric:`
> `1. The CSV contains a "price" column with only numeric values, no currency symbols.`
> `2. Every section header from the OUTLINE appears as an H2.`
> `3. No claim is stated without a cited source line.`
> `If any criterion FAILS, output "REVISE:" followed by a bullet list of exactly what to fix. If all PASS, output "APPROVED".`
> `OUTPUT: {{paste output}}`

The rule that makes it work: 

write "The CSV contains a price column with numeric values," not "the data looks good." Vague criteria produce noisy evaluations because the grader scores each one independently.

 And to validate before production, 

generate a few outputs manually, grade them yourself, then run the grading agent and see if it agrees. If it doesn't, the rubric needs work.

**Source:** MindStudio / InventiveHQ — https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/claude-outcomes-feature-rubric-grading-agent-powerpoint-quality · https://inventivehq.com/blog/claude-agents-outcomes-rubric-grading

---

## 5. (Broader AI world) MCP goes stateless July 28 — your servers get simpler to scale, and a 12-month clock starts

Not Claude-specific: the protocol underneath most agent tooling is having its biggest revision. 

The release candidate is available today and the final specification ships on July 28, 2026.

 The practical win: 

a remote MCP server that previously needed sticky sessions, a shared session store, and deep packet inspection at the gateway can now run behind a plain round-robin load balancer, route traffic on an Mcp-Method header, and let clients cache tools/list responses.

 Nothing breaks immediately — but 

it starts a 12-month deprecation clock for older protocol versions still running in production.

**Try this** — Concrete migration steps if you operate an MCP server:
1. Install the beta SDK now — 

beta releases of the Python, TypeScript, Go, and C# SDKs are available with support for the 2026-07-28 spec.

2. 

Migrate off initialize / Mcp-Session-Id to the new _meta envelope.

3. 

Check your auth implementation against the tightened OAuth and OIDC guidance.

If you're on the GitHub MCP server you're already covered — 

all tier 1 SDKs have preserved backwards compatibility and shipped beta support, so you don't need to do anything to maintain support.

**Source:** Model Context Protocol Blog / GitHub Changelog — https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28-release-candidate/ · https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-23-github-mcp-server-supports-the-next-mcp-specification/

---

## 6. Voice mode now inherits your text model — run Opus reasoning by voice

Quick but genuinely useful daily-driver change. 

With the new update, voice mode picks the last model people used in the text chat and uses its fastest version by default

, and 

users can choose between Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models

 — a shift from the old Haiku-only voice that 

provided quick responses but wasn't well suited for complex work.

 The beta also lets you 

talk through real work, switch models mid-conversation, and move from conversation to doing.

**Try this** — Before starting a voice session on something that needs reasoning (planning, debugging logic, drafting strategy), open a text chat and switch the model selector to **Opus** first — voice will inherit it. For quick factual back-and-forth, leave it on Haiku/Sonnet so you get faster responses. You can also switch models mid-conversation without restarting.

**Source:** TechCrunch — https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/23/anthropic-updates-claude-voice-mode-with-more-capable-models/

# This Week in AI: A Global Briefing

## 1. China's Moonshot AI ships Kimi K3, a cheaper open model that's rattling the US industry
**Region: China / International**

Chinese startup Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, and it has quickly become one of the week's biggest stories in the industry. 

Moonshot says the model closes the gap with leading US offerings and surpasses OpenAI and Anthropic's most capable systems on some benchmarks; while it still trails Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol overall, it beat models that sit just behind the leaders on benchmarks including coding and general agents.

 The significance is less about raw scores than economics and openness: 

the release of a powerful open-source model by a Chinese startup has fueled accusations of theft while forcing uncomfortable discussions about whether American tech could face an existential challenge, because it can be accessed at a fraction of the cost.

 Real adoption is already following — 

Chinese AI systems are gaining ground worldwide because they are more affordable and increasingly efficient, and US companies like Coinbase say they're switching to Chinese models to trim costs.

*Source: CNBC — https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/17/moonshot-ai-kimi-k3-model-openai-anthropic-china.html*

## 2. News Corp countersues Brave over AI scraping — a test case for publisher rights
**Region: US / International (WSJ, The Times of London, Australian titles)**

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp filed a countersuit against browser-and-search company Brave, a case that media companies everywhere should watch. 

News Corp accused the search engine of "flagrant theft" for allegedly scraping and reselling copyrighted Wall Street Journal and New York Post articles to AI companies, and is seeking an injunction, damages, and up to $150,000 per infringement.

 

In its complaint, News Corp alleged Brave masks its web crawlers so publishers cannot detect or block them, and delivers "summaries" that are verbatim or near-verbatim copied content to enterprise customers, primarily AI companies.

 The case matters because it could set precedent for the whole publisher-AI dispute: 

the countersuit is designed in part to establish a legal precedent that could reshape licensing negotiations, and if the court rules Brave's activities exceed fair use, it would strengthen publishers demanding payment for AI training data.

 Notably, News Corp is fighting and dealing at once — 

it has also struck a US$150 million deal with Meta, showing the company is pressing its legal claims while monetizing some AI use on its own terms.

*Source: Semafor — https://www.semafor.com/article/07/21/2026/newscorp-accuses-search-engine-brave-of-ai-copyright-infringement*

## 3. France's competition regulator built its own AI agents to audit the market
**Region: EU (France)**

In an unusually hands-on move, France's Autorité de la concurrence published a major opinion on the AI-agents market. 

On 17 July 2026 the authority adopted Opinion 26-A-05 on the competitive functioning of the AI agents sector — its first contribution to move downstream from model training to the deployment layer, where "agentic" AI tools reason, plan and execute multi-step tasks with limited human intervention.

 What sets it apart methodologically is that 

the inquiry, which started in January 2026, saw regulators build and deploy their own AI agents, running them through 550 shopping-related prompts to see how these systems actually behave in the wild.

 The concentration findings are stark and directly relevant to any business relying on these tools: 

the advisory opinion found that OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic together control more than 84% of the AI agent market.

 Regulators flagged risks including 

platformisation, disintermediation and algorithmic collusion, and called for full enforcement of existing rules, interoperability and open standards.

*Source: MLex — https://www.mlex.com/mlex/artificial-intelligence/articles/2502571*

## 4. Gulf states go operational: UAE and Saudi Arabia move from AI ambition to deployment
**Region: Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia)**

The Gulf's AI story this week shifted from spending headlines to actual production use. 

According to Confluent's 2026 Data Streaming Report, 38 percent of organisations in both the UAE and Saudi Arabia have agentic AI solutions running in production, placing the Gulf among global leaders in translating AI ambition into operational reality.

 Underpinning this is heavy state strategy and infrastructure: 

the UAE has invested through its National AI Strategy and a growing ecosystem of AI institutions, while Saudi Arabia continues to accelerate investment under Vision 2030.

 The regional consulting and data-centre push remains active this week, with 

Deloitte Middle East describing how AI is changing the game for regional consulting amid geopolitical uncertainty and rising competition, tied to data centre investments and the wider AI push in the region.

 For media and creator businesses, the takeaway is that the Gulf is emerging as a serious market and infrastructure hub outside the traditional US–China axis.
*Source: Khaleej Times — https://www.khaleejtimes.com/business/tech/uae-saudi-arabia-lead-global-race-to-put-autonomous-ai-to-work*

## 5. Databricks raises ~$3B at a $188B valuation, betting on AI governance and agents
**Region: US**

On the funding side, data and AI platform Databricks closed one of the week's largest rounds. 

Databricks closed a strategic funding round led by Coatue, raising roughly $3 billion and pushing its valuation to $188 billion — up from $134 billion previously.

 The money is targeted rather than general: 

the funds are going toward three product areas — Unity AI Gateway, which handles governance across multiple AI systems; Genie, which connects data to automated actions; and Lakebase, built for AI agent workloads.

 The direction reflects where enterprise demand is heading — 

the valuation jump reflects sustained enterprise demand for AI infrastructure, with product focus squarely on governance, cost control, and agentic tooling.

 For media companies weighing their own AI stacks, it's a signal that the market is now pricing in "control and orchestration" layers, not just raw models.
*Source: AI Weekly Pulse (Ink & Algorithms) — https://inkandalgorithms.systeme.io/ai-weekly-pulse-4-ai-model-releases-july-2026*

tracks.body:
# Cross-Spectrum Political Briefing — Week of July 20–27, 2026

Three stories dominated the week, all with direct 2026 midterm relevance: the escalating US–Iran war, the administration's new replacement tariffs, and a court filing in which the government conceded it canceled clean-energy grants concentrated in Democratic states. For each, the neutral factual anchor comes first, followed by the three framings.

---

## Story 1: The US–Iran war escalates as Congress splits on war powers

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

A US bombing campaign against Iran continued for roughly 13 consecutive nights after a ceasefire agreement collapsed earlier in July.

 

On Thursday, the Senate voted 47-49 to kill a joint War Powers Act resolution that would have forced Trump to end hostilities, while the House earlier that day cleared, 214-208, a concurrent resolution aimed at pushing Trump to abandon the war.

 

Even if both chambers passed similar measures, the concurrent resolutions lack the force of law.

 

Gas prices rose again, with the national average for a gallon reaching $4.11 on Saturday, up 11 cents in a week.

 By week's end, strikes appeared paused amid renewed diplomacy.

### 1. Progressive framing
**The New Republic — opinion/commentary** — https://newrepublic.com/post/213486/trump-iran-war-horrible-new-reason-worry
The left-leaning read emphasizes strategic futility and personal impulsiveness. 

The piece cites Wall Street Journal reporting that at a White House meeting Trump launched into a tirade against Iranian leaders and is worried the war is "consuming his presidency," with an official saying Trump sees few good options besides continuing daily strikes.

 

It argues the strikes aren't having much impact militarily or psychologically, pointing to satellite images showing Iran rebuilding damaged sites quickly.

 The framing: an open-ended war of choice with no exit, driven by ego rather than strategy.

### 2. Neutral framing
**CNN — news reporting (live blog)** — https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/26/world/live-news/iran-war-trump

Wire-style reporting notes strikes appeared to remain paused after nearly two weeks of nightly bombing and Iranian attacks on US allies, with UN Ambassador Mike Waltz saying Trump is giving talks "some space."

 

It reports Waltz acknowledged "a lot of stockpiles are depleted" while insisting the US has "everything that it needs," and that Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine had raised concerns about munition levels needed for a major escalation.

### 3. Conservative framing
**National Review — opinion/commentary** — https://www.nationalreview.com/2026/07/a-war-restrained-by-the-people/
Notably, a leading conservative outlet is critical rather than cheerleading. 

The piece's thesis is that Trump's ambitions are being checked by the American voter.

 Separately, the traditionally conservative Wall Street Journal editorial board has argued from a hawkish direction — that Trump's on-and-off approach signals weakness and that Iran believes it can outlast a president who no longer wants the fight (https://thehill.com/homenews/media/5874592-trump-iran-us-response-ceasefire/, opinion). Note these two conservative critiques point in opposite directions: one says the war is too unpopular to sustain; the other says Trump hasn't been forceful enough.

---

## Story 2: New "replacement" tariffs take effect on 60 trading partners

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

Sixty trading partners, including all of America's most important ones, now face tariffs of 10% to 12.5%, with the new duties taking effect at 12:01 a.m. ET Friday.

 

The tariffs cover trading partners accounting for 99% of America's imports and replace expiring temporary tariffs in place since February.

 

The new levies replace stopgap tariffs imposed after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs in February, and were issued under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

 

The administration says the 60 economies failed "to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor."

### 1. Progressive framing
**NPR — news reporting** — https://www.npr.org/2026/07/24/nx-s1-5905783/trump-tariff-trade-global-canada
NPR's account (framed neutrally but emphasizing legal defiance) leads with the president's reaction to the courts. 

It reports that on the day the Supreme Court ruled against a broad swath of Trump's tariffs he was visibly angry and determined to enact more anyway, saying "Other alternatives will now be used to replace the ones that the court incorrectly rejected."

 

It notes those "alternatives" referred to other laws the administration might use after the Supreme Court said the president's preferred IEEPA route was unlawful.

 The progressive-adjacent read: an end-run around a Supreme Court loss.

### 2. Neutral framing
**NBC News — news reporting** — https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/trump-tariffs-60-countries-forced-labor-rcna588972

The US trade representative announced a wave of tariffs on dozens of economies to replace Trump's temporary 10% tariff, which expired at midnight ET.

 

NBC notes that in February the Supreme Court struck down most of Trump's tariffs imposed under IEEPA, ruling the administration exceeded its authority.

 

It gives the opposing side directly: key trading partners such as the EU strongly rejected the forced-labor accusation, with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas comparing EU and US labor laws.

### 3. Conservative framing
**ABC News — news reporting** — https://abcnews.com/Business/trump-set-impose-sweeping-tariffs-60-trade-partners/story?id=135020049
The framing most favorable to the administration foregrounds its stated legal rationale. 

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the 10% to 12.5% tariffs were aimed at combatting "forced labor" violations.

 

The finding of wrongdoing followed an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits levies in response to an adverse trade policy taken up by another country.

 

This framing also stresses that a series of exemptions would significantly ease the measure's impact.

**One factual caution for the reader on all sides:** the "forced labor" justification is the administration's stated legal hook to survive court review after IEEPA was struck down; the affected partners include long-standing allies like Canada and the UK, and the EU disputes the characterization. Treat the forced-labor rationale as a contested legal claim, not an established finding.

---

## Story 3: Administration concedes clean-energy grants were canceled in states that voted against Trump

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

In a court filing this month responding to a lawsuit by University of California researchers, the administration acknowledged that it terminated nearly 300 federal research grants, and that the filing was made in response to the cancellation challenge.

 

The Energy Department sent OMB a list of more than 600 grants it recommended canceling from recipients in states where Kamala Harris won and that have two senators caucusing with Democrats, and OMB ultimately terminated 284 grants in October 2025.

 

A DOE lawyer conceded that, with one exception, the 284 terminated grants were in states that voted for Harris with two Democratic-caucusing senators, and acknowledged none were included based on "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor."

### 1. Progressive framing
**The New Republic — opinion/commentary** — https://newrepublic.com/post/213526/trump-team-admits-defunding-states-didnt-vote-for-him
The progressive read casts this as an admission of political retaliation. 

It notes OMB Director Russ Vought called the money "Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda" and singled out projects in 16 blue states, and that only a month earlier Energy Secretary Chris Wright had angrily told a House committee the cuts "did not involve politics," calling the accusation "bullshit."

 

The framing's core point: a DOE lawyer then "conceded the obvious."

### 2. Neutral framing
**NBC News — news reporting** — https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-administration-concedes-canceled-research-grants-blue-states-rcna589129

NBC reports that from a list of more than 2,300 awards, OMB identified 284 to terminate in October 2025, and that a DOE official wrote that with one exception the terminated grants were in states that awarded electoral votes to Harris and have two Democratic-caucusing senators.

 

It also reports that a remaining 340 grants proposed for termination were ultimately not canceled.

### 3. Conservative framing
**Reason — opinion/commentary (libertarian)** — https://reason.com/2026/07/27/the-energy-department-admits-the-omb-canceled-grants-solely-to-punish-trumps-political-opponents/
Notably, the libertarian-right outlet does not defend the move — it condemns it. 

Reason recounts that DOE recommended canceling 624 clean-energy grants approved under Biden, and OMB winnowed the list to 284, all but one awarded to projects in states represented by Democratic senators that voted for Harris.

 

It quotes Energy Secretary Chris Wright insisting "No decisions were made on politics" and calling the charge "bullshit," then concludes that while that may have been true of DOE's original list, it was not true of the terminations OMB approved.

 A pro-administration defense on the merits (that the grants were wasteful "Green New Scam" spending) exists via Vought's public statements, but the factual admission in the filing undercuts the claim that the final selection was apolitical.

**One factual caution for the reader on all sides:** The administration's public defense — that this was simply cutting wasteful clim
